notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [א] ״שֶׁמַּקְרֶבֶת״ אוֹ ״מְבִיאָה גְּאֻלָּה לְעוֹלָם״, וְזֶהוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת ״מְבִיאָה רְפוּאָה״
notes.body_html: Yoma 86b: “R’ Yochanan said: Great is teshuvah, for it brings [some texts: hastens] the redemption, as it says, ‘and a redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those of Yaakov who turn from transgression’ (Yeshayah 59:20) — why does ‘a redeemer come to Zion’? Because [there are] ‘those of Yaakov who turn from transgression.’” R’ Tzadok: redemption is the outward spreading of teshuvah’s rectification-going-forward — deliverance from the enslaving kingdoms, as healing is from the inner “leaven.” The Zohar makes the connection between teshuvah and geulah even more structural. Zohar, Nasso 4:29, explains that sin distances the final heh of the Divine Name from the vav; this separation is expressed below in the destruction of the Mikdash and Israel's exile among the nations. Consequently, "כל מאן דעביד תשובה, גרים לאחזרא ה' לאת ו', ופורקנא בדא תלייא" - whoever performs teshuvah causes the heh to return to the vav, and redemption depends upon this. It concludes: "הכל תלוי בתשובה... ואין הדבר תלוי אלא בתשובה, דאיהו שלימו דשמיה" - everything depends on teshuvah, for teshuvah is the completion of His Name. Thus the Gemara's language that teshuvah "brings the redemption" is not only causal in the ordinary sense. In the Zohar's language, the inner repair accomplished by teshuvah and the historical repair called geulah are two expressions of the same reunion: what is restored within the Divine Name is manifest outwardly as the return of Israel and the rebuilding of the place from which they were exiled. This also supplies a bridge to the earlier simanim. There the higher teshuvah was described as restoring the Divine Name "as before"; here the same restoration spreads out into history. The personal and national processes are therefore not separate topics. The inward healing of the relationship becomes, when it reaches its full extension, the redemption of the community and the world.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §4): “Anyone who wishes to sanctify himself and comes to purify himself may merit the beginning of redemption [aschalta d’geulah], which is ‘the gate through which the righteous enter’ — the rung of Yosef HaTzaddik, who in all his ‘imaginings’ had intent for the sake of Heaven; that his wishing to be a king and ruler, as his brothers charged, was for the sake of Heaven — to draw down abundance and sustenance to them through himself, for he knew he was the ‘channel’ of the influx.” The se’if’s redemption: the spreading-out of the healing-middah — “the gate through which the righteous enter,” the drawing-down of God’s influx into every good.

notes.body_html: Berachos 17a: “The Sages of Yavneh would say: Master of the Universe, it is revealed before You that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents? The leaven in the dough [se’or she-ba’isah, the yetzer] and the enslavement to the kingdoms.” R’ Tzadok: healing addresses the “leaven” within; redemption addresses the “enslavement to kingdoms” without. Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Pesachim 104a:1, quotes this very prayer - "רצוננו לעשות רצונך ומי מעכב, שאור שבעיסה ושעבוד מלכיות" - and uses it to define the inner identity of a Jew. In explaining havdalah, the Izhbitzer says that beneath the external "form and garment" there is an immense holiness fixed in the heart of every Jew: "אבל באמת הוקבע בלב כל אחד מישראל קדושה עצומה." The se'or and the foreign rule obscure what is already present; they do not create a second, equally authentic will. This fits R' Tzadok's division exactly: the leaven is the internal obstruction that healing removes, while the kingdoms are the external obstruction that redemption removes. In both cases what emerges is not a newly manufactured Jewish will, but the will that was present underneath the obstruction all along. Sefas Emes, Pesach 27:2, places the two obstructions in one chain. The admixture of good and evil introduced through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge is "שאור שבעיסה," and "מזה בא כל הגלות" - from this comes the entire exile; therefore, he says, Chazal regularly place "שאור שבעיסה ושעבוד מלכיות" together. On Pesach the matzah represents a momentary Divine suspension of that admixture: before the dough could become leavened, the light of holiness appeared and Israel went free. He adds that the first Exodus is the preparation and continuing power for the last redemption: "יציאת מצרים שהי' ראשית הגאולה, בכח זה יכולין לעורר תמיד הגאולה." R' Tzadok's sequence - healing first, geulah as its spreading outward - is almost diagrammed by this Sefas Emes: the inner admixture generates the outer exile, and its clarification opens the road to redemption. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 14, gives the same point from the side of avodah. The beinoni can tell himself that he does not truly wish to become a rasha or be separated from Hashem, because of the hidden love "כמו בלב כללות ישראל"; even the lightest Jew can surrender his life for Kiddush Hashem, and ordinary sin occurs only because a "ruach shtus" makes him imagine that the act does not sever that bond. This is a useful Chabad parallel to the Izhbitz formulation: the deepest will belongs to holiness, while the obstructing layer is real and must be fought, but is not the soul's final identity.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §17): the se’or she-ba-isah [leaven in the dough] “is that which prevents [us], as it says (Berachos 17a), before Hashem; and through [matan Torah] one merits the Torah, which is the tavlin to the yetzer — to use it only according to His will.” This is §4-1’s own proof-text unfolded: “our will is to do Your will, and who prevents? The leaven in the dough” — the inner will of the seed of Yaakov is wholly for God, and the se’or is only the alien intruder; the Torah given at Sinai is what disarms it, so the hidden will can act unhindered.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Ohr Zarua LaTzadik §1): “all Israel who stood at Har Sinai — their zuhama [pollution] ceased — meaning the zuhama that the serpent injected [into Chavah], which is desire [ta’avah], in the language of the Sages.” This is §4-1’s freedom “at the time of matan Torah… from the yetzer hara”: the serpent’s ta’avah — the very “leaven in the dough” that alone keeps Israel from acting on “the will to do Your will” — was, at Sinai, lifted away; that is the “healing” of the soul’s own illness, before the sin brought the pollution back.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 38a: “‘And the sons of Yechanyah: Asir, She’altiel his son’ (Divrei HaYamim I 3:17); another explanation: ‘She’altiel’ — that God took counsel [nish’al] with His court [about relaxing the oath against Yechanyah’s line]; ‘Zerubavel’ — that he was sown in Bavel [nizra b’Bavel]. And what was his [real] name? Nechemyah ben Chachalyah.” R’ Tzadok: Zerubavel/Nechemyah, of David’s seed, is the redeemer who sprouts within the exile. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Prophets, Zechariah 4:1, takes the prophecy addressed to Zerubavel - "לא בחיל ולא בכח כי אם ברוחי" - as a prophecy of the very end of redemption. He contrasts Avraham and Yitzchak, whose service shook the worlds through mighty human exertion, with Yaakov, who said "האלקים הרועה אותי מעודי" and would not make even a small movement until Hashem took him by the hand and led him like a sheep after its shepherd. That, the Izhbitzer says, is "נחלת יעקב": looking and waiting for Hashem's salvation with such complete dependence that one never departs from His will. "וזהו יהיה סוף וקץ הגאולה, שיתמעטו כל הכחות מפעולות אדם, רק השי"ת יעזור את בית יעקב" - this will be the end and completion of redemption: the powers attributed to human action will recede and Hashem Himself will help the house of Yaakov. Hence Zechariah's word specifically to Zerubavel, "not by army and not by strength, but by My spirit." This is an especially close Izhbitz-Radzin companion to R' Tzadok's choice of Zerubavel as the first disclosure of this fourth rung. Zerubavel is not merely a political figure who happens to arise in Bavel. His very prophetic sign is that redemption germinates where visible power is weakest, so that the redeemer's emergence from the place of exile becomes a demonstration that the saving force was hidden there from Hashem from the beginning. The point must not be read as passivity in the revealed duties of Torah; the same Ishbitz tradition insists that a person must do what is commanded. It is, rather, the final interpretation of the success: even the strength with which one acted is recognized as "כי אם ברוחי.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §21): “the wise understand that it is a complete miracle and a complete redemption — yet it was not in complete revelation before all flesh; and therefore this festival is called, in Scripture’s language, simcha [joy].” This is exactly §4-2’s “already began… but its completion is in the future”: the redemption of the Second-Temple era — the light that “already began through Zerubavel ben She’altiel, of David’s seed” — was a true redemption, yet still hidden, awaiting the open revelation that only the Mashiach of David’s seed will bring. Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayeshev 19:3, describes precisely the reduced but real Davidic light of the Second Temple period. After the first Mikdash was destroyed, "נגנז גודל התקיפות הזה," yet "אור מלכות בית דוד היה מאיר עוד אור מצומצם" - the light of Davidic kingship still shone in contracted form, and Zerubavel, governor of Yehudah, stood at Israel's head. The Beit Yaakov distinguishes a holiness fixed openly in the body from a holiness present only in a more hidden, service-dependent form; the Second Temple belonged to the latter condition. This supplies an Ishbitz vocabulary for R' Tzadok's claim that the fourth greatness of teshuvah truly began with Zerubavel yet had not reached its final expansion: it was genuine Davidic light, but "מצומצם," a contracted disclosure awaiting its future completeness. Chiddushei HaRim, Vayigash 2, supplies the complementary view from the end of the process. When Yaakov discovered that Yosef was alive, he saw retroactively that the years of concealment had been for good; the Chiddushei HaRim writes that at the complete redemption it will likewise become visible "למפרע שכל עניני הגלות היה לטובתינו, ויתברר איך ומה כל פרט ופרט" - retroactively, all the matters of exile will be seen as having been for our benefit, and the role of every detail will be clarified. He adds that before the enslaver was born, the last redeemer was already born in the line of Yehudah and Peretz: Hashem "מקדים רפואה" before the wound. This gives powerful content to the siman's link between teshuvah and geulah. The final redemption is not merely exit from exile; it is the historical analogue of teshuvah's rectification of the past, when the very story of exile is reread and its hidden redemptive seed is disclosed.

notes.body_html: Pesachim 118b: at the Splitting of the Sea, the angel of the sea protested casting the Egyptians onto dry land (so Israel could see them dead): “‘is there a slave whose master gives him a gift [the spoils/the sight] and then takes it back?’” R’ Tzadok adapts the principle: once Israel is “handed over” to a nation for the moment, a distinct judgment is needed to overcome that nation and extract them — the work of teshuvah’s forward-guarding.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §9): “as soon as Moshe Rabbeinu came and aroused them, they immediately believed in Hashem — and by the merit of emunah they were redeemed; that is, through this the light was aroused, little by little, within their hearts, until they merited to go out from darkness to a great light, for emunah is the beginning of the apprehension of the light of His Shechinah.” This is §4-3’s ruling that “the Egyptian redemption was not through teshuvah at all”: it turned on faith, not repentance — the bare belief that opened them to the light of the Torah they were “yet to receive,” redemption granted on the credit of a will not yet acted upon. Sefas Emes, Shemos 15:5, gives a particularly apt explanation of the faith that preceded the Egyptian redemption. On "ויאמן העם וישמעו" he asks why the verse does not first say that they heard and only then believed. He answers that this is like Israel's "נעשה ונשמע": the good middah is already rooted in Jewish souls, and it accompanies them even in exile, only there it exists in the form of emunah. "גם קודם השמיעה היו מאמינים ומצפים לישועת ה'... רק בגלות עיקר העבודה באמונה" - even before the hearing they believed and waited for Hashem's salvation; in exile the essential avodah is faith. After redemption that hidden quality becomes revealed action. This sharply illuminates R' Tzadok's distinction here between the redemption from Egypt and the later redemptions that follow sin and require teshuvah. Egypt was the birth of the nation before the Torah's regime of transgression and repair had been established. What existed was the latent holy orientation of Israel expressed as faith and expectation; the Exodus carried that hidden emunah into revelation, preparing "na'aseh ve-nishma" at Sinai. In this sense the first geulah is not yet the fruit of teshuvah but the revelation of the root from which later teshuvah becomes possible.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 119:106: “נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי וָאֲקַיֵּמָה, לִשְׁמֹר מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ” — “I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous ordinances” — David HaMelech, in the great alphabetical psalm. In its plain sense (Rashi, Radak) David binds himself by oath to observe the mitzvos. From this verse the Gemara (Nedarim 8a) derives that “one may swear to fulfill a mitzvah in order to spur himself on [le-zaruzei nafshei]” — and this although every Jew already “stands sworn from Har Sinai” (mushba ve-omeid mi-Sinai), so that a further oath adds no formal obligation; the Ran explains that it nonetheless takes effect as a permitted, even praiseworthy, device to strengthen oneself in avodas Hashem. R’ Tzadok grounds Nechemyah’s enterprise in this verse of his ancestor David: the renewed “re-accepting of the Torah” — coming “to the sealed document with oath and vow” — is precisely the oath as a forward-looking zeruz, the engine of the teshuvah of fences and safeguards.

notes.body_html: Rus 3:13: “לִינִי הַלַּיְלָה, […] אִם יִגְאָלֵךְ טוֹב יִגְאָל, וְאִם לֹא יַחְפֹּץ לְגָאֳלֵךְ וּגְאַלְתִּיךְ אָנֹכִי, חַי ה׳; שִׁכְבִי עַד הַבֹּקֶר” — Boaz to Rus on the threshing floor: “Stay the night… if he will redeem you, good, let him redeem; but if he does not wish to redeem you, then I will redeem you myself, as Hashem lives; lie down until morning.” In its plain sense (Rashi) Boaz swears to act as redeemer and reassures her to remain in modesty until morning, “that it not be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.” R’ Tzadok relies on the aggadic reading (cited in the sefer as Sifrei; the extant midrashic locus is Vayikra Rabbah 23:11, and cf. Rus Rabbah): that all that night Boaz was assailed by his yetzer, and his oath “chai Hashem” was sworn against his yetzer — “he swore to his yetzer” that he would not touch her unlawfully. This is the ancestral root (Boaz → David → Nechemyah) of “swearing to fulfill a mitzvah” and to subdue the yetzer — binding oneself by oath as a fence against sin, the very counsel Nechemyah publicized throughout Israel. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Matos 2, treats the very phenomenon R' Tzadok cites here - swearing in order to overcome the yetzer - as a specific Torah remedy for the moment when ordinary counsel no longer works. The Izhbitzer distinguishes the advice of Avos, "look at three things and you will not come to sin," which operates before desire surges, from the crisis "בעידנא דיצר הרע לית מאן דמדכר ליצר טוב," when the yetzer suddenly overwhelms a person. For that hour the Torah gives the counsel of neder: "חי ה' אם אעשה זאת לעבור על רצון השי"ת חס ושלום." He then cites precisely David and Boaz, "שליצרם נשבעו," and joins to them the nazir of Shimon HaTzaddik who swore, at the moment his vanity flared, to shave his beautiful hair for Heaven. This is a strong Izhbitz explanation of why the fences and oaths of this se'if belong to the rung that brings geulah. The oath does not declare the yetzer unreal; it recognizes that there are moments when inner knowledge has been eclipsed and therefore creates a revealed boundary strong enough to carry the person through the eclipse. That is the opposite of misusing Divine foreknowledge to excuse the act. The hidden Divine story is left to Hashem; at the point of bechirah the person strengthens the revealed command with an additional fence. Nechemyah's communal enactments are the national form of the same medicine that David and Boaz applied within themselves.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 59:20: “וּבָא לְצִיּוֹן גּוֹאֵל, וּלְשָׁבֵי פֶשַׁע בְּיַעֲקֹב, נְאֻם ה׳” — “And a redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those of Yaakov who turn from transgression, says Hashem” — from Yeshayah’s prophecy of the redemption. Rashi: the redeemer comes to Zion for the sake of “shavei fesha,” those who turn back from sin. This is the Gemara’s very proof (Yoma 86b) that “great is teshuvah, for it brings [hastens] the redemption” — the go’el comes because of the ba’alei teshuvah. R’ Tzadok binds the complete redemption to “shavei fesha be-Yaakov” specifically: it comes through the turning-from-sin of the seed of Yaakov, and “be-Yaakov” precisely — for “He did not do so for any [other] nation”; the complete rectification of the soul belongs to Israel and not to the nations of the world.

notes.body_html: Devarim 32:12: “ה׳ בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ, וְאֵין עִמּוֹ אֵל נֵכָר” — “Hashem alone did guide him, and there was no foreign god with Him” — from Shiras Ha’azinu, of God’s lone guidance of Israel. Rashi: “Hashem badad yanchenu — He guided them securely, alone, in the wilderness, with no foreign god’s aid; and so is He destined to settle them, dwelling alone and secure”; “ve-ein imo el nechar — none of the gods of the nations had any power to display strength and wage war against Him” (cf. Onkelos). “Badad” bespeaks Israel’s singular separateness and security under God alone (cf. “am levadad yishkon,” Bamidbar 23:9). R’ Tzadok reads it of the complete redemption: “Hashem badad yanchenu” — Israel alone, with no admixture of the nations and “no foreign god with Him” — for the nations have no portion or existence in the ultimate redemption of the soul, which is “badad,” Israel’s alone; as against the days of Mashiach, when the nations still retain “some joining” so long as they have existence. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Ha'azinu 5, comments on this exact verse, "ה' בדד ינחנו ואין עמו אל נכר," that in this world many created things can appear as aids to Torah - wealth, possessions, and the conditions that broaden the mind - "אבל לעתיד לא יהיה שום כח רק השי"ת לבדו": in the future there will be no power at all except Hashem alone. This brings the siman's final contrast into unusually sharp focus. The complete geulah is not only that hostile powers cease to rule; even helpful secondary powers cease to claim independent standing. "Badad" means that the redemptive order is experienced directly as Hashem's guidance with no rival or auxiliary power beside Him. Taken together with the Mei HaShiloach on Zechariah cited above - "לא בחיל ולא בכח כי אם ברוחי" - the Ishbitz picture forms a single arc. Zerubavel inaugurates a redemption whose secret is already that human force is not the final cause; in the complete future that truth is totally manifest, "ה' בדד ינחנו." This is why R' Tzadok can describe the fourth rung as a spreading-out of teshuvah: the same recognition that, after return, uncovers Hashem's presence within the individual's story ultimately expands until the national story itself contains no alien power standing outside His guidance.
